questions.question: Why can BM25 miss a document about automobile repair for the query `car mechanic`?
options: It scores lexical evidence and does not inherently equate `car` with `automobile`
It discards the rarest query term before scoring, and `car` is the rarest here
It normalizes by document length, which penalises long repair manuals heavily
It requires every query term to appear at least once in a matching document

questions.question: Which change addresses simple morphological variation more directly than semantic mismatch?
options: Adding an approximate nearest-neighbour index over dense vectors
Applying stemming or lemmatization in the analyzer
Raising the inverse document frequency weight on rare terms
Expanding each query term with its corpus co-occurring neighbours

questions.question: A support query describes a symptom while the relevant article names its cause. Which retrieval weakness is most likely?
options: The query is too short to produce a reliable length normalization
The article ranks below shorter documents that repeat the query terms
Query and document express related meaning with different vocabulary
The analyzer stems the symptom words into a form the index lacks

questions.question: Why can broad synonym expansion reduce precision?
options: It dilutes the inverse document frequency of the original query terms
It lengthens the query so length normalization penalises every candidate
It shifts scoring onto expanded terms that appear in fewer documents
It can introduce unintended senses of ambiguous terms into the query

questions.question: A corpus is dominated by queries containing exact invoice IDs. Which design judgment is strongest?
options: Retain strong lexical retrieval, because exact identifiers are hard evidence
Move entirely to dense retrieval, since identifiers embed as distinctive tokens
Expand each identifier to numerically adjacent IDs to improve recall
Strip identifiers at index time so scoring focuses on descriptive text

questions.question: Which evaluation best establishes that vocabulary mismatch harms candidate generation?
options: Compare mean reciprocal rank before and after the reranker is enabled
Measure labeled recall at a cutoff, segmented by query type
Track how often the top result changes when synonyms are added
Sample queries where the exact-match path already returns a good answer

questions.topic: LSA as a Bridge: SVD on the Term-Document Matrix
questions.question: What matrix does latent semantic analysis decompose?
options: A term-by-term matrix of corpus co-occurrence counts
A document-by-document matrix of pairwise cosine similarity
A weighted term-document matrix over the corpus
A query-by-document matrix of historical click-through rates

questions.topic: LSA as a Bridge: SVD on the Term-Document Matrix
questions.question: What does keeping the largest k singular values produce?
options: An orthonormal basis in which every term is mutually independent
A sparse index whose postings lists are truncated to k entries
A clustering of documents into exactly k labelled topics
A rank-k approximation of the original term-document matrix

questions.topic: LSA as a Bridge: SVD on the Term-Document Matrix
questions.question: Why can LSA place `car` and `automobile` near one another?
options: Their corpus co-occurrence patterns load onto similar latent directions
The decomposition consults a synonym lexicon while factoring the matrix
Terms of similar corpus frequency are assigned adjacent coordinates
Stemming has already collapsed both surface forms into one row

questions.topic: LSA as a Bridge: SVD on the Term-Document Matrix
questions.question: What happens when k is chosen much too small?
options: The reconstruction becomes exact, so rare distinctions dominate the space
Broad latent themes merge distinctions that relevance depends on
The representation grows sparser and reverts to lexical matching
Documents collapse onto the axes, making cosine similarity undefined

questions.topic: LSA as a Bridge: SVD on the Term-Document Matrix
questions.question: Why does classical LSA handle polysemy poorly?
options: It weights each term by frequency, so ambiguous terms are down-weighted
It requires singular vectors to be non-negative, collapsing distinct senses
One term row combines evidence from every sense of the word
It builds one decomposition per document, so senses never align globally

questions.topic: LSA as a Bridge: SVD on the Term-Document Matrix
questions.question: A large changing corpus is refactored after many new documents arrive. Why might old LSA coordinates shift?
options: Cosine similarity is recomputed against a different set of neighbours
New documents extend the vocabulary, so existing rows are re-indexed
The weighting scheme rescales each column as document lengths change
The global term-document decomposition itself has changed

questions.question: What does a learned text encoder output for single-vector dense retrieval?
options: A fixed-dimensional vector representing the whole input text
One vector per token, which the index stores and searches separately
A sparse weight over the vocabulary, like a learned term expansion
A similarity score against every document already in the index

questions.question: Why can contextual layers distinguish two senses of `bank`?
options: Each sense is trained as a separate entry in the model's vocabulary
A token's representation depends on the tokens surrounding it
The encoder resolves ambiguity by consulting the document's title
Ambiguous tokens are split into sense-specific subword units

questions.question: What must happen after changing the embedding model used for a document index?
options: The approximate index parameters must be retuned for the new recall curve
The lexical statistics must be rebuilt so hybrid fusion stays calibrated
Every document must be re-embedded into the new coordinate space
The similarity metric must be switched from cosine to inner product

questions.question: Why can one vector for a 100-page manual retrieve poorly?
options: The encoder's positional limit truncates the text before the vector is formed
Long documents accumulate norm, so they dominate every similarity ranking
Approximate indexes degrade as the stored vectors grow more distinctive
Pooling many subjects into one vector hides the relevant local passage

questions.question: A dense retriever returns topically similar but unauthorized documents. What is the correct remedy?
options: Apply current ACL filters independently of the semantic similarity score
Train the encoder so unauthorized documents embed far from user queries
Raise the similarity threshold until unauthorized results fall below it
Index each tenant's documents with a tenant-specific embedding model

questions.question: Which evidence most strongly supports adding dense retrieval to a production hybrid system?
options: Nearest-neighbour probes show semantically related documents cluster well
It improves labeled candidate recall on paraphrase-heavy query segments
The encoder outperforms the previous model on a public benchmark suite
Latency stays within budget once the approximate index is fully tuned
